text: The email was four lines long, and Gerald read it three times standing at the kitchen counter, his coffee forgotten beside the toaster. Your position has been reviewed. Effective immediately. He had given that company nineteen years. He had trained the men who now sat in his old chair and drafted the safety protocol the regional office kept waving in front of auditors. Now a twenty-eight-year-old in a fleece vest would be walking the floor with a cardboard box and a lanyard. Gerald's jaw locked. He went to the garage and started hitting the heavy bag his son had left behind, one blow, then another, until the chain rattled against the rafters and his shoulder burned. His wife called his name from the house. He did not answer. Anger moved through him like a current with nowhere to ground itself. He wanted to drive to the plant and say every true thing he had held back for years, about the shortcuts and the ignored complaints, about the foreman who had lied to a widow. Instead he stood in the cold garage and breathed through his teeth, watching his knuckles split, while the fury kept climbing the walls.

Long-time lurker, first post. My landlord just served me a notice to raise rent 28 percent with 30 days' notice, after two years of refusing to fix the boiler. Three separate work orders, all closed as 'resolved' by his property manager without anyone coming out. I have photos of the mold. I have the city inspection report from 2022 that he never mentioned. And now he thinks he can price out a family with two kids in school two blocks from the library. I'm furious. Not the polite letter kind of furious. The kind where I've been drafting replies at 2am that would get me sued. My wife says I need to pick one thing and do it. So here's the plan: I'm filing a tenant complaint tomorrow, and I'm going to tell the council rep exactly what this man is. Does anyone know how to cite the local rent stabilization ordinance? I want the words 'retaliatory' and 'bad faith' in writing. Also, if you know a lawyer who'll take a case on contingency and actually answers the phone, please DM. Anger is useful right now, so I'm going to use it.

Dad, I'm writing because I can't stand in the same room as you right now without saying something I'll regret, so here it is in ink. You told the whole family at Thanksgiving that I'd thrown away my law school place. You said it while Mum was carving, in front of my cousins. I was so angry I left the table, and I'm still angry three weeks later. I left law school because I was miserable, and because I wanted to build the thing I'm building now, which you have never once asked me about. You do not get to rewrite my decision to make yourself look like the wise one. I'm also furious that you called Anna to ask whether I'm 'stable.' She told me. That's a betrayal, and you know it. I'm not asking for an apology letter, I know how that goes. I'm asking you to stop talking about me as a project you failed to finish. Until you can do that, I'd rather we keep our calls short. I love you. I am also furious with you, and both of those are true this week. Sam

Monday. Third time this month the printer jammed on the report I'd asked them to fix a week ago. Stood there yanking paper out of the rollers, hot in the face, while Ruth from accounts stepped around me like I was a broken chair. Came home and the kitchen light was on and the dishwasher had been run with nothing in it but a single coffee cup. Nobody's cup. Took it and put it in the sink and turned the tap so hard the water hit the back of the basin and sprayed my shirt. Stood there soaked. Didn't say anything when Jamie came down for water. Jamie said 'Mum, what's wrong' and I said 'nothing' in the flat voice I hate. Later the landlord's text about bin day. I typed a reply that said exactly what I thought of him, all capitals, then deleted every word and sent 'Noted', which is somehow worse. Pulled the cushions off the sofa and punched one until the seam split. Feathers on the rug. Swept them up with the good dustpan. Didn't cry. Didn't sleep either.

The referee's whistle went twice and Tomas kept running toward the touchline, his boots slipping on the wet grass. Thirty-one years old and still playing Sunday league because nobody had told him to stop. The defender's elbow had come up into his ribs, clean as a surgeon's, and the ref had waved play on. Now the parents on the sideline were shouting, and his teammates were pulling at his shirt. He shook them off. The defender was laughing, actually laughing, pulling his socks up. Tomas stepped in close enough to smell the cheap spray deodorant and said nothing at all. His hands stayed open at his sides. He could feel his pulse in his teeth. Across the pitch his son stood by the bench, hugging a water bottle, watching his father with a face that had gone very still. Tomas looked at the boy and turned away. He walked to the corner flag and kicked it over and stood there with the pole in his hands, breathing through his nose, until the ref blew for half time and the whole field began to move again around him.
